links.note: 931 forbids wanting gambling even when one wins (வேண்டற்க வென்றிடினும்), because the winnings are like the hook's metal a fish swallows (தூண்டிற்பொன்). 177 opens with the same வேண்டற்க and forbids the gain of coveting (வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம்) because its fruit is hard to make good when it ripens (விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கு அரிதாம் பயன்). Both judge a gain by what it does to the gainer afterwards, in dice and in coveting.

113 says to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 931 uses the same concession, 'even if you win' (வென்றிடினும்), and still refuses the gain, calling it a swallowed hook. In both the apparent success of a wrong source is conceded and set aside.

932 asks whether gamblers, who get one and lose a hundred (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும்), can have any way to live well. 463 says those with understanding do not take up a deed that loses the capital for the sake of a gain (ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை). The gambler is the plain case of the trade 463 rules out in the planning of any undertaking.

931 compares what is won to the hook's metal swallowed by a fish; 932 then counts the cost: one gained, a hundred lost. Parimelazhagar ties them, reading the 'one' of 932 as that hook-bait, which keeps the player at the table in the hope of more.

933 says that if one keeps calling the rolling dice-throw (உருளாயம்), wealth and its income (பொருளாயம்) go and fall outside (புறமே படும்); Parimelazhagar takes 'outside' as into enemies' hands. 1009 says the wealth a miser gathered without love, self-regard or virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The gambler and the hoarder, by opposite habits, both end with their wealth in strangers' hands.

385 defines a king as one able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it and apportion it (இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலும் காத்தலும்). 933, which Parimelazhagar reads of a king, says both the gathered wealth and its sources (பொருள் ஆயம்) leave him if he keeps at the dice. One habit undoes the gathering and the guarding that 385 makes the mark of rule.

934 says nothing gives poverty like gambling, which does many small harms and ruins standing (சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும்). 1045 says that within the one affliction called poverty many sufferings arrive (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்). Read together they form a chain: gambling brings harms on the way to poverty, and poverty then brings its own.

935 says those who clung (இவறியார்) in pride to dice, gaming hall and skilled hand became people with nothing (இல்லாகியார்). 437 uses the same word of the miser: the wealth of one who clings (இவறியான்) without doing what should be done perishes. இவறுதல், holding on and not letting go, ends in loss in both verses, whether the thing held is money or the game.

539 advises thinking, when swollen with one's own joy, of those who were ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). 935 supplies such a memory: those who took pride (தருக்கி) in the dice and came to nothing; Parimelazhagar reads them as kings of former times and names the Pandavas. 935 does for gambling what 539 asks a ruler to do in general.

936 calls gambling முகடி, the goddess of misfortune, and says those she covers (மூடப்பட்டார்) will not fill their bellies and will suffer. 617 says the same goddess (மாமுகடி) lives in sloth, and the lotus goddess in the effort of the one without sloth. The book gives misfortune a residence twice: in idleness and in the dice.

167 says the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). 936 names that sister, முகடி, as gambling itself, covering those who play. Envy hands a person over to misfortune; gambling, in 936, is misfortune under another name.

937 says time spent in the gaming hall ruins long-held wealth and character (பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்). 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's தோல் (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்), which Pope takes as dignity of speech. The two sentences have the same shape: an inherited standing and a personal quality lost at one stroke, with gambling as a cause and poverty as a cause.

938 lists what gambling does: it destroys wealth (பொருள் கெடுத்து), makes one take up lying, destroys compassion (அருள் கெடுத்து) and drives one through misery. 248 ranks two of these losses: those without wealth may flower again one day (பூப்பர் ஒருகால்), but those without அருள் are finished. By 248's measure the third item in 938's list is graver than the first.

757 calls அருள் a child born of love that is raised by the wealthy foster-mother called பொருள். 938 has gambling destroy both பொருள் and அருள். Parimelazhagar assigns the losses in 938 to separate causes (losing, winning, resentment), but 757 suggests a link between them: with the nurse gone, the child is harder to raise.

939 names five things, among them learning (கல்வி), that 'அடையா' the one who takes to gaming. Parimelazhagar glosses this as 'do not come to him', but Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take the five as departing from him. On that second reading 939 conflicts with 400, which calls learning the wealth that cannot perish (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்); on Parimelazhagar's reading there is no conflict, since the gambler never acquires it.

166 says the kin of one who envies a gift perish without anything to wear or eat (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் இன்றி). 939 begins its list of what gaming keeps away with the same pair, clothing and food (உடை ... ஊண்). Envy and gambling are both measured by the loss of the plainest necessities.

370 says craving has a nature that is never filled (ஆரா இயற்கை), and that giving it up yields a nature that does not shift. 940 shows that unfilled nature at work: the game is loved more with every loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும்), and the living being's love grows with every suffering (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்). That the love is for the body is Parimelazhagar's and Pope's supply; Kalaignar takes it as love of life.

In 1145 a lover says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is wanted more each time one is drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்). 940 has the same 'each time ... the more' construction with another vice, the dice, as the comparison (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்). The lover uses the figure to praise his state, while 940 uses it to describe an attachment fed by its own losses.

941 says the three humours counted by the learned, beginning with wind, cause disease whether they exceed or fall short (மிகினும் குறையினும்); Parimelazhagar refers the excess and shortfall to food and activity. 466 says one is ruined by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செயக் கெடும் ... செய்யாமையானும் கெடும்). Both verses locate harm on two sides of a right amount, in the body and in action.

942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats after making sure that what was eaten has been digested (அருந்தியது அற்றது போற்றி உணின்). In 1326 a lover says that digesting what was eaten is sweeter than eating (உணலினும் உண்டது அறல் இனிது), and likens sulking before union to it. The lover's figure takes for granted the rule that 942 states as medicine, and turns it from health to pleasure.

943 says to eat knowing the measure once digestion is complete, as the way one who has a body can carry it long (நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) seems to exist and then perishes; Parimelazhagar refers that measure to one's wealth. The same phrase governs both the stomach and the purse. (This edition prints 'அறவறிந்து' in 943; Parimelazhagar's gloss reads அளவு அறிந்து.)

943 treats keeping the body going for long as a goal and gives the means. 968 asks whether a life of nursing the flesh (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is any medicine (மருந்தோ) once one's greatness has lost its dignity. The chapter on honour sets a limit to the chapter on medicine: prolonging the body is not worth having at that price.

943 speaks of 'one who has gained a body' (உடம்பு பெற்றான்) and how to make it last; Parimelazhagar adds that a human body is hard to gain. 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is excess (உடம்பும் மிகை). The two address different people, householder and renouncer, and 345 marks where 943's care for the body stops applying.

no_link_reason: Its content (compatible foods, eating only after real hunger) restates the chapter's rule; I found nothing outside the chapter that it genuinely connects to beyond what 942 and 943 already carry.
A dietary rule (compatible food, eaten with restraint, மறுத்துண்ணின்) with no counterpart elsewhere that goes beyond the general theme of measure already linked from 941, 943 and 947.

links.note: 946 says disease stays with the one of very great feed (கழிபேர் இரையான்), as pleasure stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்). 420 asks what it matters whether those live or die who know taste only by the mouth and not by the ear, and calls them மாக்கள். Both verses use a word with an animal sense for the person ruled by the mouth: இரை, feed, and மாக்கள்.

947 says that if one eats greatly without discerning the measure of the fire within (தீயளவு), disease arises without measure (நோயளவின்றிப் படும்). 475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if they are piled too high (சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). In both a fixed capacity, the digestive fire or the axle, is what excess breaks, whatever the quality of the load.

289 says those who know nothing but stealth do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்). 947 says the one who eats beyond the measure of his fire gets disease beyond measure. Chapter 29 uses அளவு as a moral measure and chapter 95 as a bodily one, and in each case overstepping it brings its own penalty.

948 sets out an order of enquiry: look into the disease, then its root, then the means that subdue it, and act so that it works (நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி ... வாய்நாடி). 504 has the same threefold நாடி for judging a person: examine the qualities, examine the faults, examine which predominates, and take that. Diagnosis of a patient and assessment of a candidate are given the same grammar of step-by-step examination before a decision.

948 tells the healer to look for the root of the disease (நோய்முதல்) before the remedy. 360 does this for suffering in general: when desire, anger and confusion perish even in name, the நோய் perishes. The chapter on true perception treats pain as chapter 95 treats illness, by naming causes and removing them.

949 says the learned healer should act after considering the patient's measure, the illness's measure and the time (உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும் ... கருதிச் செயல்). 471 says to act after weighing the strength of the deed, one's own, the opponent's and the allies' (தூக்கிச் செயல்). Both end in செயல் after a list of things to be sized up against each other: the patient's capacity against the disease, as one's own strength against the enemy's.

516 tells a ruler to examine the doer, examine the deed, and act in keeping with the time (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 949 gives the healer a matching three: the patient, the illness and the time. Person, matter and moment are the terms of judgement in delegation and in treatment alike.

637 says that even when one knows the method of doing a thing, one should act knowing how the world goes (செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்); Parimelazhagar glosses the method as what the treatises teach. 949 addresses the one who has learned (கற்றான்) and still requires him to consider this patient, this illness and this moment. Both hold that book learning has to be fitted to the particular case.

950 divides medicine into four parts: the patient (உற்றவன்), the healer, the medicine and the attendant. In 1102 a lover first states the ordinary rule, that the remedy for an illness is something other than it (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற), and then says that for the illness she causes she is herself the medicine (தானே மருந்து). The lover's point depends on the separation of roles that 950 lays out, and collapses cause and cure into one person.
